Naive

/nah-EEV/ — rhymes with believe · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Someone who is naive lacks experience or good judgment and is too trusting or easily misled.

Naive about city life, he handed his suitcase to a friendly stranger.

Worked Example

Naive about city life, she accepted a ride from a kind-seeming stranger at the train station and nearly lost her wallet.

Naive captures not just her inexperience with city dangers but her vulnerability to being misled — she trusted someone she shouldn't have. Simply calling her 'inexperienced' wouldn't show the dangerous trusting quality that makes naive so precise.

How Naive Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

gullible

gullible: easily tricked into believing false claims

innocent

innocent: unaware of dishonesty; pure of intent

credulous

credulous: too quick to believe without proof

Antonyms

sophisticated

sophisticated: experienced and very hard to deceive

worldly

worldly: wise from wide real-life experience

How Strong Is It? — inexperienced → innocent → naive → gullible

inexperienced vs. naive

inexperienced vs. naive: Inexperienced is the mildest word here, weaker than naive: an inexperienced person simply has not done something yet, while a naive person's lack of experience leads them to trust too easily.

innocent vs. naive

innocent vs. naive: Innocent is gentler than naive: an innocent person is merely unaware of dishonesty, while a naive person's overly trusting nature actually makes them easy to mislead.

gullible vs. naive

gullible vs. naive: Gullible is stronger than naive: a naive person may be fooled because they lack experience, but a gullible person will swallow almost any story, however far-fetched.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — naïf (from Latin natus, 'born')

Root — naïf (from Latin natus, 'born'): natural, untaught, just born (Latin via Old French)

Put it together

Put it together: Naive came through French naïf from Latin natus, 'born': it originally described someone natural and untaught, showing only the judgment they were born with — which is why it now means lacking the experience to spot deception.

Use the root in a new word: natural

Use the root in a new word: natural: A natural talent appears without any training — natural and naive both grow from Latin natus, 'born,' since a naive person shows untaught, untrained judgment.

Word Choice

neutral

Naive means too trusting because you lack experience — you're open and honest in a risky way. Use it when someone believes too easily or fails to see danger because they haven't learned to be skeptical. For someone simply unfamiliar with a topic, 'inexperienced' is more accurate.
